rewrites.blindSummary: This country is dangerous for trans visitors. Sodomy is criminalised (1 year, both sexes — a domestic-origin law, never under historic administration); a legislator is seeking support for a harsh 2024 anti-homosexuality bill (so far unsuccessful); mob violence is documented; no legal gender recognition.
rewrites.blindTangential: Sodomy criminalised (1 year, both sexes) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2024 bill (not passed) signals trajectory.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Active hostile bill (2024) not yet passed.
blindSourceSummaries: A news outlet (16 Oct 2024): a legislator is seeking support for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill filed that summer; related proposals would imprison children as young as 10 years old for gay sex — documents an active legislative threat beyond the existing statute.

A joint international report (April 2020): a participatory review and analysis of the legal, social and human-rights environment for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity in this country.

A news outlet (9 Apr 2012): anti-gay sentiment growing since a major foreign government announced plans to promote LGBT rights abroad; new legislation proposed longer jail time for homosexuality and a group distributed fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

A news outlet (19 Mar 2012): the country's president defended laws criminalising homosexuality in a joint interview; her remarks drew international comment on the country's stance (a foreign figure declined to comment).

rewrites.blindSummary: This country is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2020 penal code criminalises acts “contrary to morality or against nature” (2 years), enforced: two women were detained in June 2024 after asking a religious official to marry them, convicted in December 2024 (released for time served). No legal gender recognition; a small, conservative nation.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2020 criminalisation and the 2024 prosecution show active enforcement of morality provisions — trans visitors are captured via birth-sex status; the case also signals risk for anyone in a same-sex relationship.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: 2024 prosecution is same-sex (climate); shows active enforcement.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying human-rights organisation country profile documents that this country criminalises same-sex sexual activity (up to 3 years' imprisonment under the penal code).
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying news report (Dec 2024) covers a couple in this country released after a same-sex sentencing verdict.

A government annual human-rights report (2023): same-sex conduct criminalised under the penal code, but authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions during 2023 and did not actively enforce the law; no non-discrimination law; police reported not to incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons and none was reported that year; widespread impunity listed among major human-rights problems. (Corrects the earlier claim: the Dec 2024 couple conviction is not in this 2023 report — it comes from the 2024 sources.)
A government 2010 human-rights report: general human-rights baseline (poor prisons, restrictions on movement/press/religion, discrimination against women) with limited LGBT-specific content.

A human-rights organisation (updated 12 Mar 2026): a penal-code article punishes same-sex acts with 6 months–2 years plus a fine (a few hundred dollars); no discrimination protections, no legal gender-marker change, no known LGBTIQ organisations (registration chilled by an association-restricting law); enforcement documented — first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy after a leaked video (2022), first same-sex arrests of two women June 2024, conviction Dec 2024 with time served; the government repeatedly refused international decriminalisation recommendations.

A news outlet (23 Dec 2024): a court on 12 Dec 2024 sentenced two women to five and six months for homosexuality and released them with time served — the couple had been arrested in June 2024 after asking a religious official to marry them; first conviction of this kind, called a human-rights violation by a human-rights organisation; the report cites a penal-code article (up to five years) as the provision.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country is dangerous for trans visitors. The penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct, but vague “good morals” provisions make homosexuality “de facto illegal” in practice; no anti-discrimination law, no legal gender recognition, no community infrastructure; authoritarian government with foreign military bases but no rights space.
rewrites.blindTangential: The “good morals” provisions de facto criminalise homosexuality — trans visitors are captured via birth-sex status and presentation.
blindSourceSummaries: A human-rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): penal-code provisions refer vaguely to 'good morals' with no explicit criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, yet its at-a-glance table still marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the country; no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register; current-fact: still no explicit offence, but 'obscene acts'/public morality provisions are used against people.

An online encyclopaedia overview (current): legality of same-sex conduct is ambiguous — no law says either way, but authorities can prosecute public same-sex conduct under 'good morals' provisions, so it is treated as de facto illegal; discrimination protection exists in employment only; no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated.

A government annual human-rights report (2023) section on sexual orientation and gender identity: law does not explicitly criminalise consensual LGBTQI+ conduct, but status and conduct are taboo; a societal pattern of discrimination with no official violence cases citable — complaints can be filed with police or the national human-rights commission; no legal prohibition of SOGI discrimination; pervasive social and religious intolerance makes people fear family and community shunning on disclosure.
A government 2015 human-rights report: general human-rights assessment (suppression of opposition, harsh prisons, FGM, trafficking) — baseline context with limited LGBT-specific content.

A government asylum-research response to an information request (research 2009–Mar 2012): documentation on treatment of sexual minorities in this country was scarce across all consulted sources, leaning on a 2010 government country report — a dated historical baseline showing how little legal/protection framework and support services existed in that period.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous legal environments. The 1983 penal code criminalises “acts against nature” with death by stoning (de facto moratorium on executions, but the statute is live); and a human-rights organisation documents that gender nonconformity is effectively criminalised through debauchery, heresy, and religious-morality provisions — trans people can be apprehended solely for their gender expression. There is no legal gender recognition, no healthcare, no community, and religious courts operate alongside the civil system.
rewrites.blindTangential: “Acts against nature” carries death by stoning (moratorium on executions, statute live) — a catastrophic formal exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying human-rights organisation country profile documents that this country criminalises same-sex sexual activity with a possible death penalty under religious law.

A human-rights organisation's country review: transgender people effectively criminalised through 'debauchery' provisions — a penal-code article carries 1 month to 2 years' jail and fines for public indecency/debauchery offences applied to gender nonconformity; grave lack of official data on the trans community.

A government annual human-rights report (2023): consensual same-sex conduct criminalised but penalties not enforced; reports of violence and threats against LGBT people; civil society objected to scant indictments and officials sometimes acted with impunity.

A news outlet (16 Jan 2026, from a human-rights organisation): the penal code keeps a maximum sentence of death by stoning for men; the government confirmed a de facto death-penalty moratorium in 2021; arrests and detentions under the provisions continue in recent years; low visibility drives stigma; since 2008 the country has served as refuge for LGBTIQ people from other countries.
A local organisation's website (2026): openly campaigns from within the country on freethinker and LGBT-adjacent causes — evidence of a minimal but real public advocacy space.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2022 penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct — but a 2024 human-rights organisation report documents twelve women imprisoned between January and August 2024 in police raids led by security forces, with detention-for-bribes and indefinite imprisonment; a draft law on prostitution and the rights of homosexuals (2020, status unclear) would formally criminalise. A long-ruling dictatorship; no recourse.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2024 raids and the draft criminalisation law target homosexuality — trans people face the same machinery via gender-nonconformity.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: The 2024 documented prisonings targeted lesbians; trans people face the same machinery via gender-nonconformity.
blindSourceSummaries: A human-rights organisation report on lesbophobia, human rights and police raids in this country: police and military intervene in spaces of assembly, expression and residence of lesbian women; police detain known lesbians collectively ('lesbians are members of a sect'), including collective punishment when one lesbian is sought.

A human-rights organisation profile (updated Mar 2026): the 2022 penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy or gender diversity, but a 2020 draft law on prostitution and the rights of homosexuals (status unclear) would effectively criminalise; authorities still apply the obsolete 1954 law on vagrants and criminals, which normalises conversion practices and classifies homosexuality as illness; three instruments institutionalise discrimination (a military justice code, a ministerial order on 'immoral' activities, provincial regulation).
A government 2021 human-rights report: same-sex conduct not specifically criminalised but LGBT persons face societal stigma; no anti-discrimination protections, within a general repression context.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country demands real caution. Same-sex conduct is legal (the common-law sodomy offence was struck down in 2012); a local rights organisation documents failures to prevent violence, harassment and discrimination by government and non-government actors (2024 submission to a periodic review); no legal gender recognition; a small organised community inside a neighbouring nation's geographic envelope.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2012 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
blindSourceSummaries: A joint stakeholder report (Oct 2024) by three rights organisations on LGBTQ+ rights in this country: documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and community-level SOGIESC discrimination; same-sex conduct is not criminalised but no protections exist.

A legal-rights organisation's submission (Nov 2024) to a periodic review: highlights LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination among three key concerns (alongside inclusive education for children with disabilities and revocation of NGO lawyers' practising certificates).

A joint briefing (Oct 2020) on legal gender recognition in this country: analysis of law and policy against international best practice; one local group is the only known LGBTI organisation in the country; researched by an academic with community consultations.

A government 2016 human-rights report: documents military mutiny arrests, torture of detainees, the killing of a senior military officer, and the LGBT section noting no criminalisation but societal stigma.

A rights organisation's paper on transgender rights in this country (2017): constitutional analysis — a constitutional clause on 'sex' and 'other status' should include gender identity per an international human-rights body; no law allows gender-marker changes; a trans person using a non-matching passport could be charged; the labour code's non-discrimination clause omits gender and sexual orientation.

The 2024 labour act (full text, via an international labour-law database): unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, forced and child labour prohibitions — the current statutory framework for workplace rights.
